BBC World News Digest: Xi greets Putin in Beijing - days after Trump's China visit
Welcome to the Global News Podcast from the BBC World Service.
Our main stories today: Russian President Vladimir Putin receives the red carpet treatment in Beijing, solidifying the close ties between Russia and China. In US politics, Donald Trump has strengthened his influence within the Republican Party after his chosen candidate secured victory in Kentucky's primary.
Delving deeper into China-Russia relations: President Xi Jinping welcomed Putin to Beijing, following a similar visit by President Trump last week. Putin's status as a junior partner is evident, with Russia becoming economically dependent on China due to international sanctions following its invasion of Ukraine. Over a quarter of Russia's exports, including fossil fuels, now go to China, providing an economic lifeline for Moscow. Putin's visit also serves to project his image alongside Xi, a key figure in global diplomacy.
Arsenal has been crowned English Premier League champions for the first time in 22 years. The title was clinched after Manchester City's draw with Bournemouth. Fans are celebrating their first Premier League win since 2004, a testament to manager Mikel Arteta's "trust the process" philosophy. Arsenal is also set to play in the Champions League final, aiming for further success.
In US politics, Donald Trump's "revenge tour" against Republican opponents saw success in Kentucky's primary. Thomas Massie, a known Trump critic, lost to a Trump-backed challenger in a race that saw over $33 million in spending, making it the most expensive House primary on record. This outcome demonstrates Trump's tightening grip on the Republican base.
A worrying Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could see suspected cases reach 1,000. Over 130 people have died. The World Health Organization warns that cuts in health funding have severely hampered response efforts. Former US CDC director Tom Frieden highlighted that the US government has weakened its defenses against Ebola, with significant staff reductions at the CDC.
In Germany, the "Ulm Five," pro-Palestinian activists, face trial for breaking into an Israeli arms company, destroying property, and using symbols of Hamas. The UK has classified Palestine Action as a terrorist group, unlike Germany, where the case highlights a unique approach to pro-Palestinian protests influenced by historical sensitivities. If convicted, they face up to five years in prison.
Football drama continues with Manchester City's Pep Guardiola expected to depart as head coach. Despite winning 17 major trophies and transforming English football's style, his final season concludes without a Premier League title.
In astonishing football news, Southampton has been expelled from the Championship playoffs. They were disqualified from the playoff final, which would have led to Premier League promotion, after admitting to illegally watching opponents' training sessions.
Finally, a peculiar humming sound from the ocean, long baffling fishermen, has been identified by SETI Institute scientists as humpback whales, possibly clearing airways or sneezing. This finding offers insights for marine conservation, potentially preventing ship collisions, and aids the search for extraterrestrial life by understanding diverse communication systems on Earth.
Good bye.

item.description:
Financial Times FT News Briefing: The EU wants a Putin whisperer
Good morning from the Financial Times. Today is Wednesday, May 20th, and this is your FT News Briefing.
Europe wants to start its own negotiations with Vladimir Putin. US-led talks on ending the war in Ukraine have stalled out in recent months, prompting European leaders to consider creating their own special envoy to negotiate with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Washington and Kyiv have both expressed support for Europe to engage with Russia in parallel to the US-led peace talks, and Russia appears to be open to the idea.
The motive for this move is twofold. First, the US-led push for peace talks has stalled, with the Iran war distracting US diplomats and a stalemate on the frontlines in Ukraine meaning no real movement. Secondly, Europeans are becoming increasingly nervous that if they are not involved in this conversation, they will be forced to accept a deal they do not have any say in. These discussions, which have bubbled around for a while, are now very much mainstream. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his administration have signaled openness to this. The Russians are at least publicly saying that they also welcome it, with Vladimir Putin's spokesperson stating they think it is great if somebody wants to pick up the phone, and they are always welcome to talk to somebody from Europe who is going to be productive. Washington also understands and is okay with Europe setting up a parallel track, and does not think it would disrupt or take attention away from the existing talks.
There are at least four leading candidates on a short list being considered to lead these talks: Mario Draghi, the former ECB president and Italian prime minister; former German Chancellor Angela Merkel; the current Finnish President, Alexander Stubb; and his predecessor, Sauli Niinistö. These are expected to be discussed by EU foreign ministers next week. Angela Merkel has the best relationship with Putin, given the time she spent negotiating with him as Chancellor of Germany, but this also counts against her in many capitals that think she was too close to the Kremlin. Ultimately, Putin has been very clear on his red lines, and Europeans are just keen for a seat at the table. With US talks stalled and on the ground in Ukraine, Europeans feel they have nothing to lose by trying to get involved and seeing if they can make a difference.
The world is also facing a fuel crisis. The US-Iran war continues to disrupt global oil supplies, and now many African countries are running out of fuel. The cost of diesel and petrol are surging as much as 46 percent in some places. In Kenya, the situation has turned deadly, with high petrol prices sparking violent protests this week, leading to four deaths. Deadly protests also hit the East African island nation of Comoros, which actually forced the government to stop raising the price of fuel. Meanwhile, in nearby Malawi, there are no more fuel reserves, so the government is now negotiating with a pan-African bank to finance imports.
J. Powell's term as Federal Reserve chair is officially over. His last day will be on Friday, when Kevin Warsh is sworn in as the new Fed chair. Powell has led US monetary policy since 2018. He was appointed by President Donald Trump, who later came to call him a "moron" among other things, especially for not lowering interest rates. Trump and Powell spent a lot of time butting heads over interest rates, and Powell will almost certainly be remembered for protecting the Fed's independence.
When Powell took the helm, the US economy was growing at a very healthy clip, with the unemployment rate close to its lowest level in nearly two decades, and the equity and housing markets doing very well. However, because the economy was doing so well, the Fed ended up raising rates, which very quickly led Trump to ponder whether Powell or China's Xi Jinping was a bigger enemy to America. The relationship carried on in a similar vein from there.
The COVID-19 pandemic hit during his tenure. The Fed's immediate response to the market panic by cutting interest rates and buying bonds is something that people really see as a strength of Powell's time. This helped cushion the economic blow from COVID. However, that plus the fiscal response from both Donald Trump and his successor as US President Joe Biden, did produce the worst wave of inflation in decades in the US.
Powell largely tended not to speak publicly about Trump's attacks on the Fed. However, that changed in January when in a very short video address, Powell directly called out the US president and stated that the threat of criminal charges related to interest rate decisions was about whether the Fed would be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions, or whether monetary policy would be directed by political pressure or intimidation. This was a real game-changer. It was heard not only by former Fed governors and central bank governors across the world, but also on Capitol Hill. A lot of Republican senators backed Powell and not the US president. Specifically, Tom Tillis, the Republican Senator for North Carolina, said he would not allow Trump's pick to replace Powell, Kevin Warsh, to move forward to a vote on the Senate floor unless the probe was dropped. So, Powell played his hand very well. He is staying on as governor, and the sense that gives me is that even though Powell has won the battle, the war for the central bank's independence from the executive branch is still at risk, and this is why he is staying on.
This has been your daily FT News Briefing. Check back tomorrow for the latest business news.

item.itunes:title: Bloomberg The Big Take: SoftBank’s $60 Billion OpenAI Bet Sparks Concerns
item.description:
Bloomberg The Big Take: SoftBank’s $60 Billion OpenAI Bet Sparks Concerns
Bloomberg Audio Studios presents "The Big Take."
There's been considerable drama lately surrounding OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman. A jury ruled against Elon Musk in his trial against OpenAI, suggesting he should have brought the case sooner. Reports also indicated a ChatGBT account linked to a shooter was internally flagged for abuse months before a killing spree. Numerous lawsuits have been filed, including one from Elon Musk, who alleges OpenAI shifted from a nonprofit to a for-profit. While a jury rejected Musk's claims, he plans to appeal. Families additionally accuse the company of failing to prevent chatbot interactions that led to violence and self-harm, with OpenAI denying liability. Internally, reports suggest OpenAI struggled to meet sales goals for ChatGBT, making investors nervous.
However, Softbank founder and CEO Masayoshi Son, a prominent Japanese investor, remains a steadfast OpenAI backer. Son is deeply committed to Sam Altman, unfazed by challenges, and believes ChatGPT will profoundly change the world, with Altman as a key driver.
Despite Son's conviction, not all Softbank insiders agree. Bloomberg sources, who requested anonymity, express concern that the relationship between Son and Altman is unequal. Son's support is described as deep, but Altman's side is perceived as purely business-driven. This imbalance is striking given Softbank's over 60 billion dollar investment in OpenAI, making it the second-largest external shareholder and Softbank's biggest single private company investment to date.
Son's dedication is being tested as the AI industry becomes fiercely competitive, with rivals like Anthropic rapidly emerging, adding uncertainty to Softbank's colossal bet.
Son, a tech investing powerhouse, is known for spotting early winners. His 20 million dollar investment in Jack Ma for Alibaba famously turned into a jackpot worth over 160 billion dollars. Son saw similar potential in Sam Altman. An initial attempt by Softbank to invest 1 billion dollars failed as OpenAI was a nonprofit not seeking investors. Son then focused on his Vision Fund, but faced significant setbacks, including a 14 billion dollar write-down on WeWork. Son publicly admitted his mistakes, stating it was "all his responsibility."
By 2022, Softbank was recovering, and OpenAI, with Altman and ChatGPT gaining immense popularity, re-entered Son's radar. Softbank shareholders questioned why the company was missing out on such a crucial AI investment opportunity. Son waited for the right moment, which arose in 2024 when OpenAI began the Stargate project for US data centers. As discussions between OpenAI and Microsoft reportedly cooled, Son seized the opening. Softbank initially invested 500 million dollars, and following a formal announcement of Stargate by President Trump, Softbank rapidly committed another 30 billion dollars, then a second 30 billion, bringing its total to over 60 billion dollars.
Son firmly believes OpenAI's language models represent the next transformational technology, his "next Alibaba." At 68, he feels time is running out for aggressive, high-stakes bets.
Son's unwavering commitment to OpenAI has raised red flags among some Softbank insiders. They worry he may be ignoring potential risks and dismissing the concerns of his lieutenants regarding aggressive expansion into AI and data center projects.
Softbank's 60 billion dollar commitment is unusual because it lacks the operational influence or a board seat typical of such substantial investments. Softbank sources find this concerning, as top OpenAI investors generally lack board representation. While Son's past allowed him direct access to founders, the dynamic with Altman is different, raising concerns about Softbank's ability to effectively voice dissent.
Softbank publicly affirms high conviction in OpenAI and emphasizes their strong strategic partnership. However, Son often employs a "gut-first" investment approach. Internally, some Softbank staff have cautioned Son that OpenAI might not meet expectations. Son's vision largely dominates Softbank; while past board members challenged him, they have since departed, leaving fewer strong voices to oppose Son's decisions when his mind is set.
These insider concerns are compounded by the rapidly shifting AI landscape and uncertainty about future defining technologies. Some investors suggest Softbank diversify by backing rivals like Anthropic, but Softbank's CFO has stated there are no such plans. Instead, Softbank has doubled down, securing a massive 40 billion dollar, one-year debt package, whose refinancing depends heavily on OpenAI's valuation maintaining a certain level.
Earlier this year, S&P Global Ratings lowered Softbank's outlook to negative, warning that massive OpenAI bets could drain liquidity and erode credit quality. While Softbank's CFO asserts financial health for refinancing, the credit market remains sensitive to its borrowing.
With OpenAI, Anthropic, and XAI all planning IPOs, intense capital competition is expected. A successful trillion-dollar IPO for OpenAI would greatly vindicate Son's aggressive strategy. However, failure could severely trouble Softbank, potentially threatening the rollover of its substantial loans. The volatile landscape and financial uncertainty make market outcomes unpredictable, embodying venture capital's inherent high-risk, high-return dynamic.

item.itunes:title: Wall Street Journal The Journal: Trapped in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Wall Street Journal The Journal: Trapped in the Strait of Hormuz
Daily cargo ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, normally 130 vessels, was less than half that last week. The Iran war has closed this vital Middle East oil export waterway, impacting the world economy. This slowdown caused serious global economic consequences. Getting ships moving again is a major U.S. strategic focus. Pressure to reopen the Strait is intensifying. Around 2,000 ships await essential goods transport. 20,000 seafarers are trapped on cargo ships and oil tankers in the Persian Gulf. Many are low-wage workers from poor countries, considered collateral damage. Their only 'crime' was their job. Life for them has become a purgatory; penned in, unable to leave for months, running out of food and water.
Before closure, 800 trade ships were in transit, many with cargo or crude oil. These ships carried only weeks of food. Sailors are from countries with little voice in the conflict. They are trained for peaceful commerce, not naval battles with drones and missiles. This became their reality with the war, catching them in crossfire. They witnessed missiles, drones, port strikes, and burning ships. Over 30 ships were hit; 10 sailors died. After a ceasefire, Iran still blocked ships. The U.S. then imposed its own blockade. Seafarers' situation is dire; some lack basic necessities, others ration supplies. All face complete uncertainty about going home. Ship owners face rising costs; some go bankrupt, impacting crew wages and supplies. Some owners stopped responding; resupplying is dangerous due to mines or fear of losing line position. Crews maintain morale by celebrating, playing games, or exercising. Many suffer depression, constantly questioning their return home. Poor cell service prevents contact with families, employers, or governments. Sailors ask reporters for news, lacking information themselves. Reporters cannot tell them when it's safe to return. Sailors receive conflicting orders from authorities. One crew, despite a U.S. military 'all clear', stayed due to Iranian threat. The conflict makes their dangerous jobs riskier. This is the third shipping crisis in five years. Many sailors have past experience with missile/drone strikes in other conflicts. Their livelihood, crucial for families, is jeopardized by danger, unpaid wages, or bankrupt owners. This crisis may be the most difficult for sailors.
When war began, Iran closed the Strait immediately. Even after a ceasefire, Iran and U.S. could not agree on reopening. In early May, the Trump administration launched 'Project Freedom'. This military plan aimed for the U.S. Navy to escort commercial ships with air support. It was seen as a low-cost, low-escalation risk attempt, but confused the shipping industry. Less than 36 hours later, Project Freedom was called off. This reversal was due to Iranian retaliation: attacks on commercial ships, U.S. Navy, and a UAE oil terminal. This was the worst escalation since April's ceasefire. Project Freedom got only two ships out, a strategic failure as Iran reasserted control. The U.S. could not guarantee safety, deterring ship owners. This showed limits of U.S. military power in the Persian Gulf. Iran's 'toll booth' strategy, charging tolls and institutionalizing control, sees minimal compliance. Iran formed the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, signaling intent to keep control. This leverage point will be difficult to resolve in negotiations. Analysts see many bad U.S. options: ongoing negotiations, Trump's threatened bombing, or repeated failed military interventions. As stalemate continues, oil prices rise, causing fuel rationing and blackouts. The longer the Strait is closed, the worse the energy shock. The acronym 'NACHO' (Not A Chance Hormuz Opens) predicts closure until severe economic consequences. The U.S. blockade tests which side withstands economic pain longer. Thousands of trapped sailors are 'hostages' of this situation. However, some argue they are not true hostages, as governments don't prioritize them like valuable assets. Discussions focus on oil flow and gas prices, not the human cost. These forgotten seafarers, who enable modern life, are deemed less important than the commodities they transport.

The AI Breakdown: 9 Codex Tips From the Codex Team
Today on the AI Daily Brief, we have a number of important updates from the AI industry.
First, Cursor has made significant strides in the AI race with the release of Composer 2.5. Cursor’s CEO previously declared "wartime" as their business model was eroded from both sides. Their top priority was building the best coding model. Composer 2.5 shows strong competitive performance against leading models like Opus 4.7 and GPT-4 on key benchmarks. The biggest differentiator, however, is cost. Cursor is serving Composer 2.5 at just 50 cents per million input tokens, and 250 per million output, making it half the cost of Opus 4.7 or GPT-4. This suggests a major performance boost comes from better reinforcement learning techniques on an existing base model, indicating significant room for leading open-source models to compete at the frontier. Cursor has also announced they are training a new model from scratch using XAI's Colossus 2 training cluster. This release is seen as creating an interesting open lane for companies to avoid becoming too locked into the large model providers.
Next, Cloudflare has published their findings after working with Anthropic's secretive new model, Mythos. Cloudflare states that "Mythos Preview is a real step forward" and that its capabilities are not just a refinement of what came before, but a different kind of tool. Two key differences were highlighted. Unlike previous models, Mythos can create an exploit chain rather than just detecting single bugs, acting more like a senior researcher than an automated bug scanner. Second, it can generate functional exploits and proofs, rather than just identifying vulnerabilities. Mythos can also test and refine its exploits if they don't work the first time. This addresses the common criticism that other models could find similar bugs, by showing that Mythos goes further to provide full code for functional exploits, demonstrating exactly what needs to be patched.
Lastly, one little bit of AI drama comes to a close. Elon Musk has lost his case against OpenAI and Sam Altman. After three weeks of testimony, the jury returned a unanimous verdict in just two hours. The jury found that Musk's claim of breach of charitable trust was barred by the statute of limitations, meaning he took too long to commence his lawsuit. Open AI successfully argued that Musk was aware of plans to form a for-profit company as early as 2018, having been sent a term sheet. The trial also surfaced Musk's own 2017 proposal to fold OpenAI into Tesla for commercial fundraising. With the core claims barred, the massive headline-grabbing tech trial fizzled into nothing, revealing much about the power struggles and internal discussions at OpenAI over the past decade.
In our main segment today, we're diving into how to maximize Codex, following tips from Jason Lu of the Codex team. The overarching goal is to enable agents to work in parallel with humans, rather than an endless series of turns.
1. Durable Threads: Use long-running, persistent threads for each key workstream. Codex's compaction system maintains context, allowing these threads to evolve like a persistent "chief of staff."
2. Voice: Utilize Codex's excellent internal speech-to-text. "The art of the ramble" allows providing rich backstories, areas of uncertainty, and messy thoughts, fostering a deeper relationship with the AI.
3. Steer: Leverage Codex's steer feature to add or update prompts mid-process without stopping the AI. This allows you and the agent to work in parallel, continuously refining as progress comes in.
4. Memory: Beyond native memory features, build structured memory. Jason uses an Obsidian vault (a file-based note system) to turn thread learnings into inspectable, editable, and reusable artifacts, keeping track of people, decisions, and project states.
5. Tools: Empower Codex with computer and browser use, as well as connectors to other systems like Slack or Gmail. This transforms Codex into an evidence-gatherer, allowing it to read files, run tests, check live documents, and interact across various environments.
6. Disentangling Work: Utilize remote control features (available in the ChatGPT app). This allows you to interact with and steer long-running projects from mobile devices, capturing fresh ideas and redirecting work without being tied to a desktop.
7. Heartbeats: Implement recurring or scheduled check-ins for threads. These heartbeats can cross tool boundaries, allowing the agent to check for updates, re-render, and post new versions in complex, multi-tool workflows automatically.
8. Goals: Use Codex’s goal feature for projects with specific, knowable, and verifiable success criteria. This pushes the agent continuously towards an objective, unlike a normal prompt which might give up.
9. Side Panel: The side panel is where Codex stops being merely a chat app and becomes a true workspace. It allows parallel processing of work by inspecting artifacts, operating web services, and reviewing changes, all while the agent is still working.
These tips collectively aim to create a continuous, parallel workflow between human and AI, avoiding the traditional turn-based interaction model.

BBC World News Digest: Desperation in Afghanistan leads to sale of children
Global News Podcast from the BBC World Service.
I'm Valerie Sanderson, and our main stories today include: Afghanistan's escalating humanitarian crisis, Vladimir Putin's visit to Beijing, and the latest on the Ebola outbreak in Central Africa.
Afghanistan is facing a desperate lack of food due to aid cuts, Taliban policies, and severe drought, pushing 4.7 million people to the brink of famine. Three out of four Afghans struggle to find food, jobs, and access to healthcare. Abdul Rashid Azimi broke down as he explained selling his 7-year-old twin daughters to feed his other children. Similarly, Said Ahmad sold his 5-year-old daughter Shaika for appendicitis surgery. In five years, Shaika will be forced to leave everything familiar to marry the son of the distant relative who bought her. We also heard reports of an increased number of child deaths due to malnutrition, with an estimated four to six children dying every month. Graveyards show twice as many children's graves as adults, a stark indicator of an invisible wave of deaths.
President Vladimir Putin has arrived in China, just days after Beijing hosted Donald Trump. Putin released a video hailing an "unprecedented level of trust" between Russia and China, stating that ties are growing economically, politically, and in defense. The Chinese Foreign Ministry, however, denied a report that President Xi told President Trump that Putin might come to regret invading Ukraine. Putin's visit sees him as the junior partner, seeking geopolitical advantages and keen to know what Xi discussed with Trump. For China, it's a political balancing act: maintaining stable ties with the West while also fostering strong relations with its friend and neighbor, Russia.
Growing international concern surrounds the Ebola epidemic in Africa. The number of deaths in the Democratic Republic of Congo has shot up to at least 131, with over 500 people infected. The World Health Organization confirmed the outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola for which there are currently no vaccines or therapeutics. In the absence of a vaccine, the WHO emphasizes crucial measures like risk communication and community engagement. The WHO is concerned that Ebola could spread outside the DRC, noting that traditional greetings involve hugging and cheek kisses, increasing the risk of transmission. Four healthcare workers have been infected within DRC hospitals, highlighting challenges in under-equipped and understaffed facilities. Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, South Sudan, and Tanzania have all heightened border surveillance and screening to contain the virus.
In Estonia, a fighter jet shot down a drone over its territory. It's believed the drone was launched by Ukraine against Russia but was knocked off course by Russian electronic jamming. Moscow claims the Baltic states are allowing Ukraine an air corridor for its attacks on Russia. A Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman, however, accused Moscow of intentionally forcing drones off course into Baltic airspace using electronic warfare. Earlier this month, two stray Ukrainian drones hit an empty oil storage facility in Southern Latvia, leading to the collapse of the Latvian government over how the incident was handled.
A nationwide transport strike in Kenya, sparked by steep increases in petrol and diesel prices, has been suspended. Protests on Monday over high fuel costs, caused by the conflict in Iran, descended into clashes, resulting in four deaths and hundreds of arrests. The strike had caused widespread disruptions with empty streets, shuttered shops, and schools, particularly in downtown Nairobi which was described as a "ghost town". This is largely due to people taking caution after violent demonstrations last year.
The US Congress is grappling with whether a victim of sexual coercion can also be an enabler. A powerful committee has been investigating four women named as potential co-conspirators of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, who were granted immunity in a 2008 plea deal. One of these women is Nadia Marcinko, a former girlfriend of Epstein. Emails reveal a complex and unequal relationship where Epstein made demands of her, and she had duties including finding other women for him. While the BBC found no evidence Marcinko recruited underage girls, victims claim she was involved in sex sessions. Marcinko's lawyer stated her entire relationship with Epstein had been coercive. Documents show Epstein referred to her as his "sex slave" and physically abused her. Her victim status has been called into question by Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna, who claims Marcinko and others were complicit. Marcinko, however, stated she was totally under Epstein's power, fearing deportation if she didn't comply. Her own emails hint at the blurry lines of her role, stating, "I do not want to be with you. But it upsets me to see you use the exact same patterns to seduce, manipulate, and ultimately control and hurt other girls."
In Spain, Jonathan Andic, son of Mango fashion retailer founder Isak Andic, has been arrested on suspicion of homicide. Isak Andic fell to his death from a cliff near Barcelona in December last year. Jonathan has always maintained it was an accident. Catalan police reopened the investigation after deeming Jonathan's testimony inconsistent with the circumstances of his father's death. Police have seized his mobile phone to examine messages sent and received at the time of the incident.
And finally, scientists have discovered and logged 1100 new marine species in the past 12 months, including ghost sharks, glass castle worms, and carnivorous tree sponges. The discoveries are part of the Ocean Census initiative, the world's largest mission to accelerate ocean species discovery. Dr. Michelle Taylor described finding a symbiotic glass castle worm, with a spiky glass structure, for the first time off the coast of Japan. These new findings are just a "drop in the ocean" in understanding complex deep-water ecosystems, with an estimated 90% of marine species still undiscovered. This knowledge is particularly pertinent in environmental debates like deep-sea mining.
I'm Valerie Sanderson, until next time, bye-bye.

The Economist The Intelligence: Spread too thin: West Africa’s next Ebola outbreak
The Intelligence Daily Briefing
Today, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern over the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The disease is a horrible pathogen with a high fatality rate, and this outbreak is particularly complicated. Africa has improved its response to Ebola in recent years, thanks to scientific advances like vaccines and better community health work. However, the current Bundibugyo strain has no known vaccine, and testing is difficult. There are also fewer healthcare workers and a weak state presence in the affected Eastern DRC, complicated by armed groups. Cuts to US public health aid, which was previously a leading contributor, have further strained resources. The US recently announced $13 million in new funding, a fraction of past contributions, and has imposed travel restrictions, signaling that Africa may be largely on its own. The response is now led by international organizations and the African CDC, which improved significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic. While African governments possess the knowledge from previous outbreaks, the institutional "immune system" of public health is sadly weaker than in the past decade.
In UK politics, Labour leader Keir Starmer is facing pressure after recent local election losses, leading to speculation about potential challengers for the prime ministership. Andy Burnham, the Mayor of Greater Manchester, has emerged as a polling favorite. However, he faces significant hurdles: he must first become an MP by winning a challenging by-election in the constituency of Makerfield, and then win a Labour leadership contest. Burnham is known for his approachable and charming style, successfully uniting diverse groups in Greater Manchester and managing significant funds. He has also shown a confrontational side when dealing with central government, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, which significantly boosted his public profile. While Burnham has several advantages over Starmer, he remains untested on the national stage, managing a small staff compared to the machinery of government. His path back to Westminster and ultimately to Downing Street will be exceptionally difficult.
Finally, we turn to the world of literary criticism. Historically, critics were often seen as "scornful" and harsh. However, a new breed of critic has emerged, exemplified by pop star Dua Lipa, who hosts a popular book club podcast. Unlike the traditional "splinter of ice in the heart" critics, Dua Lipa genuinely loves books and storytelling. Celebrity book clubs, including those by Reese Witherspoon and Gwyneth Paltrow, have gained immense popularity. Publishers benefit from increased book sales, and readers gain guidance in choosing "actually good" books from the millions published annually, many of which are dull or bad. Yet, some critics question celebrity motives, suggesting they're merely building personal brands or using books as accessories for social media. For instance, Dua Lipa was photographed licking her copy of Margaret Atwood's biography, and Marilyn Monroe's famous pose reading James Joyce's "Ulysses" sparked a decades-long debate on whether she was truly reading it. While some criticism borders on intellectual snobbery, dismissing celebrities as incapable of serious thought, some skepticism is justified. While celebrities like Dua Lipa and Reese Witherspoon genuinely enjoy books, others in the book club space offer "effortfully worthy" advice or "drivel." Ultimately, the rise of book clubs presents a paradox: reading rates are declining, but discussions about reading are booming. Perhaps, instead of listening to people talk about books, it's best to simply sit down, open a book, and silently enjoy it.

New York Times The Daily: A Trump Dissenter Fights for His Political Life
Welcome to The Daily briefing.
This episode plunges into the contentious political landscape of Kentucky, where President Trump is orchestrating a high-stakes campaign to unseat Republican Congressman Thomas Massie. Trump's motivation is clear: to maintain an absolute stranglehold over the Republican Party, ruthlessly purging any perceived disloyalty. His method involves leveraging mid-term primaries to impose ideological conformity, a strategy he's seen succeed in other states.
Massie, a seven-term incumbent, has earned Trump's ire by repeatedly defying the president's wishes, exhibiting what reporter Robert Draper describes as a "cheerfully uncaring" attitude towards Trump's directives. Massie's brand, cultivated since the start of his political career, is that of an unyielding individualist, a fiscal absolutist who famously declares, "I'm doing my own thing here." This maverick stance extends to opposing foreign aid, including for Israel, and challenging interventions in Venezuela and Iran, positions that set him apart from most Republicans.
The core of Trump's animosity, however, stems from Massie's pivotal role in forcing the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files. While Trump himself was reluctant, Massie championed the cause, forming a bipartisan coalition, and effectively became "the public face of it." His determination was so great that Trump was ultimately compelled to offer "reluctant support" for the legislation, a moment of perceived defeat Trump "clearly did not forget nor forgive Massie for."
To challenge Massie, Trump has hand-picked Ed Gallrion, a Navy SEAL veteran and dairy farmer, who has wholeheartedly embraced the role of a Trump loyalist. Gallrion's campaign is singularly focused on unwavering support for the president, promising to be a "team player" in Congress, contrasting sharply with Massie's defiant independence. This stark difference was evident at their respective campaign events. Massie's town hall, though sometimes chaotic, allowed for direct, Socratic challenges to his independence, where he confidently asserted, "You are my bosses here in Kentucky," and reminded voters he was the one who got the Epstein files released, an act Trump deemed "a borderline act of treason." Gallrion's event, by contrast, was a carefully controlled affair where he pledged to serve "wherever the coach says," equating governance to a team sport, implicitly deferring to Trump and Speaker Johnson.
This primary represents a critical juncture for the Republican Party. If Gallrion wins, it signals an unchallengeable presidential authority, where no dissent, no matter how principled or aligned with purported party values, will be tolerated. If Massie, against the odds, prevails, it could embolden other Republicans to push back against Trump's iron grip.
However, a deeper implication emerges: regardless of the outcome, Trump achieves his goal. If Massie loses, the message is clear: opposing the president incurs a severe political cost. If Massie wins, the message to other Republicans is equally stark: "do you really want to go through what I just went through in the name of independence from Trump?" The answer, as Robert Draper suggests, is likely no.
This entire saga unfolds as broader electoral "storm clouds are gathering" for Republicans. Recent polls indicate a significant Democratic lead on the generic ballot, suggesting the party could lose the House in the midterms. Despite this, Trump continues to wield unprecedented leverage, compelling unwavering loyalty, even if it means "steering this car off the midterm cliff." The question remains: how much will fear of Trump's formidable command dictate the future of the Republican Party, even in the face of political peril?

Financial Times FT News Briefing: Inside a Lebanese village under Israeli occupation
Good morning from the Financial Times. Today is Tuesday, May 19th, and this is your FT News Briefing.
The legal spat between the world's richest man and OpenAI is over for now. Bonds all over the world aren't doing so hot. Plus, we'll hear from someone living in a Lebanese village occupied by Israel.
A California court dismissed Elon Musk's case against OpenAI yesterday. The jury determined that his suit fell outside the statute of limitations. Musk, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman, and President Greg Brockman all co-founded the company as a non-profit. Musk says the other two breached their contract with him by turning it into a for-profit entity. Musk donated 38 million dollars to the group before leaving after a power struggle in 2018. The decision is a huge win for OpenAI. The legal case loomed over its plans to go public in the coming year. The financial hit could have been massive. Musk was looking for 134 billion dollars in damages and he may still get it. He said yesterday that he will appeal the verdict.
Bond yields are up across the globe. In some places, including the U.S. and Japan, they are reaching record highs. It's a sign that investors are worried about the state of the global economy, specifically, they're worried about inflation. Bonds have been selling off fairly consistently since the war in Iran started, but we saw quite a sharp sell-off at the end of last week, and some of that has carried on into this week so far. Investors are getting more and more worried about a possible inflation surge coming from the war in Iran. The Strait of Hormuz is still closed, which is much longer than most investors had expected when the war began. The idea of a looming energy shortage would push prices up across the world. This is really adding to fears that we might see proper inflation, which would cause higher interest rates from central banks and has prompted quite a nasty sell-off in the bond market in the last few days. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed now for a lot longer than most investors had expected when this all began. There was a sense last week of that really hitting home for a lot of people in the market. Also, we had a few inflation data points coming out of the U.S. which were a lot uglier than maybe had been expected and gave some early signs that this really is feeding through into the U.S. economy and the rest of the world. We also had other stories going on around the world which were bad for bonds, like the political turmoil in the U.K. We've also had quite sharp selling in Japan because there's the prospect of the government borrowing more money to fund its new budget there. In the U.S., the 30-year bond yield, which is the kind of very long-term government borrowing, was at the highest point it's been since the financial crisis in 2008 last week. This does matter for families, and it means that mortgages are more expensive, it means that for small businesses, borrowing money is getting more and more expensive. This isn't just a bond market phenomenon; this really is starting to be felt in the economy as a whole. The thing that we're all watching is the Strait of Hormuz and whether that reopens. If the strait doesn't reopen and we do get to that point of actual energy shortage, oil shortage, that will undoubtedly have an effect on inflation and also on growth, and it'll be hugely significant for the bond market as well as the rest of the market for stocks as well.
There's a new power powerhouse in the United States. NextEra Energy will merge with its rival Dominion Energy. The new company will be worth 420 billion dollars. The deal is the fourth largest of all time. It comes as there's booming demand for electricity to power AI data centers. The new utility giant would have a customer base of more than 10 million homes and businesses from Florida to Virginia.
Israel's land grab in the Middle East is growing. The FT calculates that it has seized about 1,000 square kilometers from its neighbors, Syria, Lebanon, and the Palestinian enclave Gaza. That's since Hamas's October 7th, 2023 attack. More than half of that seized territory is in Southern Lebanon, and despite a ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out air strikes there almost every day. Nearly 3,000 people have been killed in Lebanon since early March, and Israeli forces are also now trying to evacuate several Christian villages in the south that they had previously promised not to touch. Ain Ebbel is one of the first Christian villages that you encounter when you cross into the so-called security zone. Israel says it's evacuating villages for this so-called security zone, but residents fear it's an indefinite occupation. We spoke to Milad Habub, a poet and a long-time teacher, who has been hit by the military presence. He described the fear of constant bombardment, the fear of being overrun by Israeli military forces. He couldn't bring himself to leave. He knew that if he left, he might never come back. If all the residents of his village leave, then there would be nothing for people to return to. His decision to stay means he's now one of thousands trapped in this security zone. It extends about 10 kilometers into Lebanon and encompasses mostly flattened Shia Muslim villages. In its war against Hezbollah, Israel has largely targeted the Shia Muslim villages of Southern Lebanon because that's considered strongholds of Hezbollah. The Israelis made vague assurances that they won't touch the Christian villages under one condition: don't harbor Hezbollah fighters. But now, despite that, residents are caught in the crossfire. In effect, what the Israeli military are doing is destroying both ways of the south. The picture that's beginning to emerge is just row after row of destroyed buildings and town centers and infrastructure. An aid group delivering necessities to the village found residents had not seen or smelled garlic, or onions, or potatoes, or apples even, in weeks. Since this effective siege has been in place, movement is incredibly restricted in these villages. There's no commerce, there's no trade, there's nothing going in or out unless it's brought in by a humanitarian convoy. Israel says it's restricting civilian movements because of ongoing military activity and a Hezbollah presence there. But it is described as being, in effect, a siege. The Israelis are sort of couching it as a security zone, they're reluctant to call it an occupation, but that's what the Lebanese government and international legal experts are saying. If they are effectively controlling movements in and out of this zone, it's for all intents and purposes, an occupation.
This has been your daily FT News Briefing. Check back tomorrow for the latest business news.

The AI Breakdown: Beating the AI Doom Cycle
Today, we're discussing the AI Doom Cycle, an emotional and cognitive journey people experience in relation to AI. This cycle has five stages: skepticism and disbelief, AI psychosis, doom desperation, real-world recalibration, and enlightened anxiety.
The first stage, skepticism and disbelief, is waning. An early example was the DeepSeek app's popularity, offering a free reasoning model many hadn't encountered, contrasting with less accessible offerings. However, much remaining skepticism comes from outdated expectations or a lack of direct, current interaction with the technology.
Moving into AI psychosis, we see initial enthusiasm. Citadel CEO Ken Griffin, who was deeply skeptical in January, recently reversed his stance. He now views AI as "profoundly more powerful" and "real," performing complex financial analysis tasks in hours or days instead of weeks or months, leading to significant productivity boosts.
This shift, however, brought Griffin to the doom desperation stage, expressing trepidation and personal depression over AI's potential to automate extraordinarily high-skilled jobs and dramatically impact society. This sentiment is widespread, with former presidential candidate Andrew Yang echoing fears that finance will follow tech in automation. Recently resurfaced predictions from Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman suggest all white-collar work could be automated in 18 months, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei forecast 10% overall unemployment and 50% for entry-level white-collar jobs. This pervasive fear has led to public anger, with commencement speakers like Google's Eric Schmidt and Tavistock's Gloria Cofield being booed for mentioning AI's transformative power, highlighting a disconnect between tech's promise and perceived threat.
The next stage is real-world recalibration, where real-world constraints temper extreme predictions. Meta recently announced layoffs impacting 8,000 employees, partly to offset other AI investments. A major driver for recalibration is a structural compute shortage across the AI supply chain. This is forcing companies like Anthropic and GitHub to transition from subsidized flat-rate pricing to usage-based token billing. For instance, some GitHub Copilot users could see their monthly costs jump from hundreds to thousands of dollars, dramatically changing consumption patterns and forcing companies back into an ROI mindset. This cost reality, as highlighted by Axios, means AI can now be more expensive than human workers, challenging assumptions about rapid, widespread automation.
Finally, we arrive at enlightened anxiety, a place of informed and specific understanding. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, in his recent commencement speech, offered an anxiety-relieving message, emphasizing human agency and the opportunity for the US to reindustrialize and create new jobs. OpenAI's Sam Altman has also shifted his narrative from doomsaying to promoting AI for human augmentation and elevating individual lives, envisioning a future where AI handles tasks, freeing people for more meaningful pursuits. This allows for nuanced policy discussions, as seen with Matthew Yglesias's proposal to mandate affordable compute for low-income agents at data centers, or Mark Cuban's idea of a federal token tax to fund federal debt and prepare for AI's unforeseen impacts. These discussions represent a more productive approach than simply fearing a "permanent underclass."
The faster we collectively move from skepticism, psychosis, and doom desperation into real-world recalibration and enlightened anxiety, the better equipped we will be to navigate the future of AI.

Bloomberg The Big Take: Where the US-China Trade Relationship Stands Now
Following the Trump-Xi summit, analysis suggests a positive tone but little clarity on pre-summit trade issues like tariffs. China's President Xi described the relationship with the US as having "constructive strategic stability," though critics questioned the "constructive" label given a rocky past. This stability could face further tests from rising energy prices and and new US levies.
The White House announced new deals, with China agreeing to buy 200 Boeing planes and $17 billion in agricultural products. This agricultural spending, combined with soybean purchases, totals about $30 billion, effectively returning US-China trade in these goods to levels from four to five years ago. Boeing shares, however, fell 5.4% after the deal, as China likely would have purchased aircraft regardless. These agricultural purchases represent levers China can control in the relationship.
In a related move, China renewed import licenses for US beef plants, which had lapsed during the trade war. However, with an existing US beef shortage driving prices up, increased Chinese demand could further inflate costs for American consumers.
Despite President Trump's claim that tariffs weren't discussed, China's Commerce Ministry reported an agreement to establish a trade council to reduce tariffs on some products. This "Board of Trade" would review non-sensitive, low-value goods like fireworks for tariff reductions. Meanwhile, the US Trade Representative is pursuing new 301 investigations into industrial overcapacity and forced labor. These investigations could legally justify new tariffs, potentially pushing the average tariff rate on Chinese imports back above 30%.
A previous moratorium on retaliatory tariffs expires in November, with no extension in sight. Current temporary 10% tariffs expire July 24th, and new 301 tariffs might be implemented then. President Xi and Trump are expected to meet again around September, with questions remaining on whether they can sustain their current détente.
On the domestic front, the process for tariff refunds from previously ruled illegal tariffs has begun. The Customs and Border Protection Agency is processing $166 billion in refunds, with $36 billion expected by mid-June. However, companies like Under Armour, which anticipates $70 million in refunds, are also facing $35 million in increased fuel and energy costs, suggesting much of the refunds will offset rising operational expenses.
US companies face layered pressures, including tariff uncertainty and rising fuel and transportation costs, which are expected to worsen. Political figures in the White House are urgently seeking solutions, concerned that escalating inflation and affordability issues could harm their standing in the November midterms.

Wall Street Journal The Journal: For Riz Ahmed, Life is a Spy Thriller
Riz Ahmed is an actor rapper and movie producer known for his roles in Star Wars Rogue One The Sound of Metal which earned him an Academy Award nomination and the TV show Bait.
Bait explores themes of self-love and the gap between who we are and how we like to be seen. The protagonist an actor aspires to be someone else making James Bond a perfect symbol for his aspirations. Ahmed noted the show also aims to capture the feeling of being brown in the West as being stuck in a spy thriller infused with surveillance and torn allegiances. The James Bond element served a double purpose symbol of aspiration and a nod to the spy thriller genre Ahmed wanted to explore.
Securing the rights to use James Bond was a significant challenge with many believing it impossible. Ahmed personally pitched the concept to Barbara Broccoli who understood that the show’s core message transcended a typical Bond story focusing instead on life feeling like one big audition.
Ahmed shared a pivotal moment in his career when he questioned whether to dedicate his life to stepping into other people’s stories or to tell his own. He felt he was putting on a mask in big blockbusters and desired to create more personal and unapologetically specific stories like Bait and Hamlet projects where he could build his own narratives and create new archetypes.
Comparing the UK and US film industries Ahmed observed that the UK with fewer resources often leans into hyper-specificity in storytelling which can lead to breakout voices. He believes this approach where limitations can spur creativity contrasts with the US industry’s focus on broad appeal.
Regarding his approach to success Ahmed stated that there isn't one universal definition. He defines success as being true to the material and as honest as possible rather than aiming for an end result. He emphasizes following his gut and personal excitement for a topic trusting that authenticity will resonate with an audience. While acknowledging the need for business awareness he finds that over-emphasizing commercial success can be detrimental.
Ahmed’s multi-faceted career as an actor rapper and producer stems from creative curiosity rather than strategic planning. He believes that in today's industry creators increasingly need to wear multiple hats managing a complete through-line from project inception to marketing. This multi-disciplinary approach is additive enriching his creative process.
Looking at industry opportunities Ahmed is inspired by the young generation of storytellers on platforms like Instagram and TikTok. However he questions how to bridge the gap between their viral content and lasting long-form storytelling. He points out that expecting creators to work unpaid during development is unsustainable and deters top talent from entering the industry. He believes in compensating people for the entire development journey not just the final product.
Ahmed views short-form content as a necessary marketing tool. For the Bait rollout he created fake press conferences that went viral sparking conversation and demonstrating the art of distilling complex narratives into concise impactful pieces.
Ultimately Ahmed hopes to inspire people by creating unapologetically specific and distinctive work just as he has been inspired by others. He believes distinctiveness is key to standing out in the current landscape.

BBC World News Digest: What we know about latest Ebola outbreak
This is an audio briefing from the BBC World Service.
An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ituri province has been declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization. It has spread to Uganda, with Rwanda and South Sudan also on high alert. Eighty people have died and there are 246 suspected cases. Health officials are scrambling to contain the unique species of the virus, for which no treatments or cures are currently available. Key measures involve public education on health and hygiene, safe funeral practices, and water and sanitation efforts. The remote, impoverished region, complicated by armed groups and a WHO funding crisis, makes response difficult. This new strain is different from a larger 2018-2020 outbreak that was eventually controlled with significant resources.
A Hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship traveling from Argentina to Cape Verde led to three deaths and dozens in quarantine. Most passengers were evacuated off Tenerife, but a 25-person crew and two medical staff remained. The ship is now in Rotterdam, where 27 Dutch citizens will quarantine at home, and others will be held for 40 days. Cruise operators state all on board are asymptomatic, and the measures are purely precautionary.
The Ukrainian military claims Russian forces are preparing a major offensive this summer, with troops nearing Konstantinovka in the eastern Donetsk region. Ukrainian soldiers, including an infantryman with call sign "Kenya" from the 93rd Brigade, have spent 225 days on the front line, known as the "kill zone," where Kamikaze drones are prevalent. Soldiers reported constant shortages of water and food, and faced extreme cold in winter, with one comrade dying of hypothermia. Another soldier, Honey, described a terrifying moment when Russians discovered his position, dropping explosives and sending drones. Despite machines dominating modern warfare, foot soldiers remain crucial for holding Ukrainian territory.
The Spanish High Court has cleared Colombian singer Shakira of tax fraud and ordered the treasury to reimburse her approximately $70 million, including fines and interest. Shakira had been battling Spain for eight years over a 2011 tax bill, arguing she did not spend the required 183 days in the country to be a tax resident. She stated she performed 120 concerts in 37 countries that year and had no home, children, or business in Spain. Shakira released a statement condemning "brutal public targeting" and "orchestrated campaigns" to destroy her reputation, hoping the ruling sets a precedent for other taxpayers.
In the Maldives, four Italian tourists and their instructor went missing after a scuba diving trip; one rescue diver later died. Four of the five bodies have now been located deep inside a cave system in Baa Atoll. Theories for the deaths include running out of oxygen, oxygen toxicity from deep diving to estimated depths of 100 meters or more, or disorientation from kicked-up sand and dust. It is unclear if they had permission to dive to such depths, as recreational permits are typically for 30 meters. This incident marks the worst diving tragedy in the Maldives.
Data centers, vast warehouses of computers, are raising concerns about noise, water use, energy demand, and loss of green space. A plan to build one of Europe's largest data centers on agricultural land north of London has sparked opposition from local residents, who mourn the loss of productive farmland and green areas. The developer, Equinix, plans extensive tree planting, green spaces, and new pathways. Equinix's managing director for the UK, James Tyler, explained that proximity to economic hubs like London is crucial for highly responsive applications where milliseconds matter, making remote locations unsuitable. He stressed the UK's need to invest in high-quality data center infrastructure for economic growth.
Police were called to Swatch stores across the UK and Paris to control crowds queuing for a new "Royal Pop" pocket watch. In Paris, tear gas was fired; a fight broke out in Milan; and a New York shopper described the scene as a "mosh pit." This new watch is a collaboration with luxury watchmaker Audemars Piguet, whose watches typically cost over $20,000. The Swatch version sells for hundreds but is already being resold at luxury prices. Watchmaker Roger Smith notes a revival in pocket watches and welcomes products that engage young people with watches, highlighting the appeal of the collaboration's history and story.
For the first time in France's modern history, beer consumption has overtaken wine. New research shows beer consumption outstripped wine by 10 million liters last year, with wine consumption falling by almost 40% over three decades. Experts attribute this shift to beer's rebrand as more glamorous with craft beers, its lower cost, and a general move towards health-conscious choices like alcohol-free options. Despite these trends and the decline of the traditional "long lunch," French people overwhelmingly still view wine as a cornerstone of their national identity and a noble product that boosts the country's global image.

The Economist The Intelligence: Equal before the law? Transitional justice in Syria
The Intelligence Briefing
Today, we bring you three main stories: the start of a pivotal trial in Syria, an ongoing look at America at 250, and a curious whisky-making boom in China.
First, to Syria, where Atif Najib, former security chief of Daraa, is on trial for murder, torture, and orchestrating massacres. This trial is highly significant, as Najib is a first cousin of Bashar al-Assad and a senior figure tied to the brutal repression that sparked the Syrian revolution. The Syrian justice system is currently in transition, with judges reportedly aiming to use international laws and treaties to address crimes for which domestic law is currently insufficient. This trial is drawing immense public attention from victims and their families. It represents a crucial test for the legitimacy of the Syrian legal system and the government's commitment to transitional justice, especially amid concerns that current President Shara's administration has incorporated former regime members, potentially undermining the process. The outcome will be watched closely for its impact on stability and the perception of justice within Syria and internationally.
Next, our "America at 250" series takes us through the Cold War, the Civil Rights Movement, and the Vietnam War. Following World War II, America and the Soviet Union became ideological rivals, sparking the Cold War. This period saw proxy conflicts, notably in Korea and Vietnam, as the US aimed to counter Soviet expansion and promote a liberal world order. Domestically, the Civil Rights Movement gained significant momentum, marked by the Supreme Court’s 1954 ruling against public school segregation and Rosa Parks' iconic bus protest in 1955. John F. Kennedy's presidency, which began in 1960, was defined by the Cuban Missile Crisis and his assassination in 1963. In the same year, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech, leading to the landmark Civil Rights Act of 1964. However, King himself was assassinated in 1968. The Space Race culminated in America landing astronauts on the moon in 1969. Meanwhile, the Vietnam War, which had escalated under Lyndon Johnson, grew increasingly unpopular, leading to America's withdrawal and a period of national self-reflection. The anti-war sentiment fueled a counterculture that challenged traditional authority. Richard Nixon, who promised law and order, was twice elected but later resigned due to the Watergate scandal. The Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v. Wade decision, legalizing abortion, marked the end of a progressive era and ignited a significant conservative backlash.
Finally, we turn to China, where there's an unexpected boom in whiskey production. Despite a general slump in alcohol sales, including wine, beer, and traditional Baijiu, approximately 50 new distilleries have been built in China in recent years by both local enthusiasts and major multinationals like Diageo and Pernod Ricard. This phenomenon is attributed to whiskey's perception as a luxury product. While the market for mid-tier goods is struggling, both very cheap and very expensive luxury items are thriving in China. Whiskey imports reached a record high last year. Chinese whiskey has also seen remarkable growth in international markets, with exports skyrocketing from 5 million dollars a decade ago to 585 million dollars last year, establishing China as a significant global whiskey exporter. Chinese distillers are blending traditional Scottish practices with local characteristics, such as using Chinese oak for aging and incorporating domestic malt. In February, China introduced its first national standards for single malt whiskey, largely aligning with Scottish regulations. These standards mandate distillation in copper pots and aging for at least three years in specific barrel sizes, signaling a commitment to quality and a clear identity for Chinese whiskey on the world stage.

New York Times The Daily: The Courtroom Showdown Between Elon Musk and Sam Altman
A high-stakes legal drama has unfolded in downtown Oakland, pitting two of the tech world's most powerful titans against each other: Elon Musk and Sam Altman. What began as a corporate dispute has spiraled into an intensely personal battle playing out in the courtroom and on the streets.
Outside the courthouse, a carnival-like atmosphere prevails. Protestors gather daily, some singing that Musk’s race to super AI could kill each and every one. Others highlight the stark contrast between billionaires arguing over Open AI while hundreds of thousands struggle to live. Inside, the scene is equally charged. With only a handful of unreserved seats, getting into the courtroom is likened to trying to get into an exclusive club, a club for people worried about the end of the world because of AI. Each day, Musk, Altman, and other AI bigwigs must walk through a gauntlet of press, fans, and detractors, a humbling procession from a holding pen to the courtroom.
At the heart of Musk’s lawsuit is a claim of betrayal. In 2015, Musk, deeply concerned about AI harming humanity, helped co-found Open AI as an altruistic, money-losing non-profit, dedicated to building artificial intelligence for the good of mankind. His co-founders, including Sam Altman, initially shared this vision. However, by 2017-2018, Altman and his team recognized the monumental resources needed for advanced AI development. The non-profit model, they realized, would not suffice. This pivotal moment led to a series of tense emails with Musk, who worried he was losing his grasp on the company. When Musk proposed integrating Open AI into Tesla, Altman refused, leading to Musk’s dramatic exit. He declared, I’m out, good luck, I’m doing my own thing.
For a time, the separation seemed amicable, with Musk even covering Open AI’s office rent for a few more months. Then, in 2022, Open AI released ChatGPT, a chatbot that unexpectedly exploded into the most downloaded app of all time, instantly making Open AI a near-trillion-dollar company. This success triggered a massive $10 billion investment from Microsoft, far surpassing the $38 million Musk had initially invested. This was the trigger for Musk’s current lawsuit and demand for $150 billion in damages, claiming his original vision for a non-profit was duped. The profound irony is not lost: Musk himself is simultaneously building XAI, his own for-profit AI company.
The trial itself has become a war of credibility. Musk’s lawyers portray him as a serial entrepreneur and visionary, like an Iron Man figure simply wanting to do good for humanity. During testimony, Musk, known for rambling in an occasionally self-effacing way, described his daily ambitions like grocery shopping and eventually taking humanity to Mars. His core argument against Altman? They're trying to steal a charity. He presented himself as the humble billionaire aiming for altruistic good, while painting Altman as a Machiavellian figure who pulled the rug out from under him at the first whiff of money.
Altman’s attorneys, however, came at Musk with ferocity, effectively melting away the humble entrepreneur persona. They accused him of being a spurned competitor throwing a tantrum, showing how he reacts when he doesn’t get his way. The courtroom gallery, filled with Musk loyalists, reacted with fist pumps and snickers, creating a bizarre cage match atmosphere.
When Altman took the stand, he presented himself as a soft-spoken entrepreneur dedicated to positive change. But Musk’s counsel launched a brutal offensive, opening with the blunt question: are you trustworthy? This was followed by a parade of evidence portraying Altman as duplicitous and untrustworthy.
Ultimately, this trial feels vibes-based. With AI itself not broadly beloved by the public, the litigation and public mud-slinging only exacerbate distrust. This isn't just about billions of dollars; it's about dragging reputations through the mud, collecting competitive intelligence, and throwing character assassinations into the public sphere. Both sides believe the stakes are existential, not just for their companies, but for the human race itself. No matter the legal outcome, the intense, ugly competition has created an irreparable stain on these leaders and the future of AI.

BBC World News Digest: Trump warns 'clock is ticking' for Iran
Here is your Global News Podcast briefing for Monday, May 18th. I'm Alex Ritson.
President Trump issued a warning to Iran amidst stalled peace negotiations, stating that unless they move fast, nothing would be left of them. He posted online that "the clock is ticking" and "time is of the essence." Republican Senator Lindsey Graham added that Tehran was testing Washington's patience, suggesting military pressure on Iran's energy infrastructure. However, Trump's threats have had little impact on Iran, which seeks a permanent ceasefire in Lebanon before any US deal. Correspondent Joel Gunter noted Trump has made similar threats before and backed down. He says these actions are part of a maximum pressure campaign to force concessions and secure a win for Trump, even as war with Iran remains unpopular in the US.
In other news, Amnesty International reports Iran is executing more people than at any time since the 1980s, weaponizing the death penalty for political repression. This includes 29-year-old Mehrab Abdollahzadeh, arrested during anti-government protests, who was executed after forced confessions and torture. Another, Irfan Shakhoozadeh, a student accused of spying, was executed after 8.5 months of torture and a televised confession. The UN fears this year's execution numbers will be even higher.
The Democratic Republic of Congo is grappling with a deadly Ebola outbreak, with over 300 suspected cases and 80 deaths. The virus, recorded in Uganda, has led Rwanda to tighten its border with the DRC. Health officials say the outbreak began when an individual, believed by the community to be a victim of witchcraft, died and their body was repatriated to a densely populated mining area, escalating the spread. Challenges in containing it include a rare Ebola strain, difficulties in contact tracing due to displaced populations, and local distrust in medical professionals who instead turn to religious leaders. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC, attributed to human contact with infected animals, particularly fruit bats, which act as a reservoir.
In Jerusalem, a parliamentary committee met to discuss rising attacks and harassment against Christians. This follows a violent incident where an Israeli settler pushed and kicked a French Catholic nun. Insults, vandalism of churches, and being spat on are daily occurrences. Christian leaders expressed concern, noting that such incidents are becoming more frequent, with Israeli soldiers also involved in anti-Christian acts in the West Bank and Southern Lebanon. During Jerusalem Day, religious nationalist youth paraded through Palestinian and Christian areas, shouting insults and vandalizing shops.
Russia attacked Ukraine's southern Odessa region, hitting residential buildings and schools, in retaliation for Kyiv's major drone offensive that reached the Moscow region. Moscow experienced its largest drone attack, hitting residential blocks and an oil facility. While some residents expressed shock and blamed Europe, Russia shows no sign of scaling back its war on Ukraine.
Finally, in the UK, several police officers protecting the Royal Family at Windsor Castle are under investigation for allegedly leaving their posts unattended or sleeping on duty. This comes as Windsor, a high-security area, hosts King Charles and Queen Camilla.
Street preaching is causing debate in the UK. In Colchester, police were called to stop an evangelical church preaching on the street. A solicitor advised that while public order legislation addresses offensive behavior, preachers can use a defense if their conduct is deemed reasonable. Some street evangelists are shifting to one-on-one engagement, offering practical help to people experiencing poverty and homelessness.

Financial Times FT News Briefing: Are we at the tipping point for global energy supplies?
Good morning from the Financial Times. Today is Monday, May 18th, and this is your FT News Briefing.
Costs to ship goods around the Strait of Hormuz are hitting record highs, and there's a very real cliff edge coming for global energy markets this summer.
The instability in the UK, which has seen more Prime Ministers than Italy since 2015, is a growing concern.
The question for months has been when the Strait of Hormuz will reopen. US military officials say Iran laid some mines, effectively halting shipping. Defense companies and marine contractors are preparing to deploy uncrewed mine-clearing systems. The UK pledged autonomous Canadian-built vessels to help reopen the waterway when conditions allow. Meanwhile, companies shipping goods by land face backlogs and extra charges, with freight rates from Shanghai to the Gulf hitting a record high last week. An FT piece highlights the impact on seafarers stuck on stranded ships.
With shipping stagnant in the strait and little oil moving out of the region, the world has been living beyond its energy means. Governments have released strategic reserves, traders drained stockpiles, and consumers cut back to cover demand. However, this summer, a real cliff edge is coming for global supplies.
The energy system is enormous and complicated. We are currently in the eye of the storm, with prices having stabilized after an initial jump, and no panic yet. Over the summer, stockpiles of various energy products will hit critically low levels, leading the system to buckle unless the war ends and the Strait of Hormuz opens, or prices rise so high that demand drops.
The energy crisis has already arrived in large parts of the world, including Asia, Africa, and poorer countries, where people are rationing fuel and working from home. For the developed world, the crisis will mean turning up at gas stations to find much higher prices, not necessarily no fuel. Nearly 80 countries have already introduced emergency measures to offset price pressures for consumers.
Global growth is already expected to take a hit this year. The longer the conflict continues, the bigger the economic hit, with some economists starting to use the 'R-word': recession. Potential recessions in multiple economies could lead to job losses, factory shutdowns, and reduced travel, as the world still relies on oil and gas. If the economy can't secure these, growth will be severely impacted.
Economists' initial base cases expected the conflict to end in weeks. This consensus is now shifting, with a growing belief that further delays will lead to economists revising models, factoring in much higher prices, and issuing dire warnings as summer progresses.
Despite the war's effect on various industries, investment firms believe business disruptions will be short-lived. Asset managers and hedge funds, including State Street and UK's Partners Capital, are continuing to expand in the Middle East, viewing it as a region where long-term expansion plans won't be derailed by the conflict. The Middle East has been a hotbed for fundraising, offering a good way to build name recognition and attract capital from global wealth.
Following UK political turmoil, focus shifts to Manchester's by-election. The result could give Mayor Andy Burnham a parliamentary seat and a potential leadership challenge to Prime Minister Keir Starmer. If Burnham wins the Wakefield by-election, things are expected to move quickly, though his success is uncertain. Starmer publicly vows to contest any leadership challenge, but privately, he may be weighing other options. A leadership contest requires 81 Labour MP endorsements. Wes Streeting, who recently resigned, has also indicated he would stand, suggesting a leadership contest of some form is likely.
Starmer aims to reset UK-EU relations within narrow parameters, ruling out rejoining the bloc or restoring freedom of movement due to immigration being a key political issue. Wes Streeting has made a "devilish" move by clearly stating his pitch is rejoining the EU, calling Brexit a "catastrophic mistake." This puts Andy Burnham on the spot regarding his stance on Europe. While Burnham suggests rejoining is possible "further down the line," actively opposing closer EU ties could hurt his leadership election chances.
UK borrowing costs hit a 28-year high and the FTSE 100 fell 2% last week, reflecting market concern over political instability. There is speculation that an Andy Burnham administration would pursue a more left-leaning agenda, adding to the instability in the UK, which has seen more Prime Ministers than Italy since 2015.
The idea that being UK Prime Minister is an impossible job is considered a "lazy argument." The Starmer administration's "original sin" was a failure to plan, with a thin agenda and reversals on many policies despite polling indicating support for ambitious reforms.
